story_text.value:
FlightTrack was my iPhone flight tracker from the early App Store days (bestselling travel app for 4 years), and I just rewrote it from scratch.

I first wrote FlightTrack as a side project in 2008. It did really well and I quit my day job and started a company around it that was bought by Expedia in 2010; Expedia retired the app in 2017. By then I had burned out and focused my energy on classical singing, which turns out to mean living in airports. But I missed the app.

This summer I started rebuilding it from scratch, with a design inspired by Paul Mijksenaar's fantastic signage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, and working with Claude to write a server in Go and an iOS app in Swift. In 2008 v1.0 took me 6 weeks of evenings/weekends; now it took about the same amount of time, but thanks to Claude, I ended up with much more functionality (e.g. inbound flight tracking) and was able to try entire design iterations as functional code rather than just mockups.

The data is way more expensive now, so it’s a $59.99/yr subscription, but I’m giving a free year to the first 100 subscribers. I'll be adding lots of features soon but wanted to get this version out for Thanksgiving travel. Let me know anything you want and I'll do my best!

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Jakob, the solo dev and founder behind Taskless.

I got tired of my AGENTS.md files being ignored or forgotten a half dozen turns into conversations. I also remembered reading someone here on HN saying we weren't using nearly enough syntax trees in our code checks. This is the result.

Taskless gives you powerful syntax tree tools with human verifiable fixtures. The CLI is MIT licensed, so running the CLI, onboarding, rule writing, and running the underlying ast-grep & Vale checks are all local. You can give it a try with:

npx @taskless/cli

and then asking your agent to "onboard with Taskless".

Under the hood, the CLI works with your agent to read your PR review comments, fixup commits, and agent files. It takes things that keep recurring and turns them into the simplest code-level enforcement that can prevent the issue going forward. By choosing code over an LLM for the runtime, there's no model once code is generated. The checks can then be committed to your codebase and enforced. I'm particularly proud of how determinism is mixed into the onboarding flow. Any time the CLI can give the agent information without letting the agent wandering the codebase, the CLI does. It results in a more consistent experience with far fewer errors. Anonymous telemetry can be disabled outright by setting DO_NOT_TRACK=1 or TASKLESS_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 in your environment (it collects CLI version, OS, the repo's org/owner, and a bit about the repository it's running in).

When the agent's done, it creates a report you can share around to show everyone there's a better way to control the output of agentic coding tools. I thought I'd include a few here from some of my favorite repos.

- Effect: https://tskl.es/gh/Effect-TS/effect/20261104/1g4gRoMmoADlysg... I specifically liked Effect because effect-bot is in the PRs fixing bugs and writing docs for the team, and they already use oxlint plugins and a TypeScript language service plugin.

- Sentry: https://tskl.es/gh/getsentry/sentry/20261016/1ZyMPva1BzaHaa5... Sentry's all open source, and David Cramer's tweeted a lot about determinism, especially now that the team is using Junior to ship code via Slack chat.

- n8n: https://tskl.es/gh/n8n-io/n8n/20261026/1C3I3yVjFyfxNFEpl4qFA... n8n has more AI driven code than the other two repos and is a good example of how bad it can get when the determinism isn't in place. Since agents tend to copy what they see from related files, problems propagate quickly.

I'd love to hear what you're doing today to keep agents behaving, or if you do kick the tires, I'd love the honest feedback.

story_text.value:
Eleria OS is a new, Debian 13 based linux distro that is both lightweight and (in my opinion) beautiful. It has been one of the most fun things I've worked on in a long time and I really didn't think it'd go this far.

Debian logs in for you and uses the X Display Manager to load a VERY stripped down Chromium, to then load the Eleria OS Login Screen.

The HTML Desktop communicates via JavaScript to a special and custom-made bridge which then communicates to Debian 13 Trixie.

This allows for the HTML Desktop and File Manager to actually show files on your system or save a screenshot.

You may find the website here: eleria.framer.website , or the GitHub here: https://github.com/eleria-official/Eleria-OS

story_text.value:
Lanlan Jam is a multiplayer DJ simulator we built for a creators' conference last month: https://jam.lanlan.site

You can put it up on a big screen, then everyone scans a QR code and queues up to take turns “coming on stage” to perform from their phones. It works at an event or your house with friends. There's also a studio mode where you can make loops and tracks on your own and save or share them.

Full disclosure: I am not a DJ and never have been, but I think what people can do with a pair of turntables is fascinating, so went deep into the world of turntables to try to re-create the experience.

This was also a test of what we can build with the primitives of Lanlan.site, the no-code website builder I cofounded. We started it partly to get back to the more creative, fun days of the Internet, when it was easy to make passion sites and share them. Sites on Lanlan are plain html, css, and js. LLMs are good at these, and we didn't want anyone tied to a proprietary framework if they ever wanted to export and move somewhere else.

When I first started building Lanlan Jam, the goal was to push a feature we call live data, simple data channels that let webhook or arbitrary data flow into a page, using the most basic infrastructure possible (which was long-polling…). As we got closer to putting it in front of a wider audience, it turned out, unsurprisingly, that we needed real websockets. So we have just built and added it (still in beta with limited access).

There's a lot more I'd love to do with this, but I wanted to see if it resonates first. Some ideas for what could come next:

- Bring your own music. Let people upload their own tracks, making sure they have the rights to do so.

- A Guitar Hero-style guide that walks you through putting down a track that actually sounds good, with highlights and touch points along the way.

- Remixing. If anyone wants to remix this site and make it better, I'm happy to make you a copy and give you access so you can keep playing with it and improving it. In the future, we’ve been toying with the idea of Git style forking (or remixing) that users could opt in to for specific sites if they wanted other people to be able to take those sites further and remix them and potentially merge them back in after improvements have been made. We are considering adding a Git back end, which would make that easier to manage.

Curious what you think. All feedback welcome!

(Edited for formatting)

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I want to show you a project which I'm using myself to save time on worktrees creation and management. My case is a bit specific because I'm normally working on a really big monorepo, where creation of a worktree takes around a minute and 20+GB of disk space. Previously I was using a pool of worktrees which were managed by my own sessions manager. It worked, but was a bit clunky and sometimes I was running out of the worktrees anyway.

As a fun side-project I decided to create a VFS for serving git branches directly from the git object store, with only one real checkout needed. I started with read only version to speed-up the reviews (I often checkout the PRs code to get LLM support) and that is very easy to do with FUSE, but it would not let me fully replace my old solution. Adding write capabilities was a bit more involved, and writing without full kernel passthrough turned out to be a few times slower. But interestingly for my workflows it does not matter. I was also running some external tests like full Linux kernel build (allmodconfig) and the performance hit vs a native build was around 2.5%. So far so good!

After building the core I realised that having VFS allows me to play with other interesting features. And I implemented a few:

- tree structure of branch dependencies; you can e.g. have branch 'api', on which 'store' and 'ui' depend. When you add or fetch new commits to 'api', whole tree rebases automatically

- read only views showing "merged" state of each node in the tree from the previous point; e.g. you can check how 'api' branch would look like, if both 'store' and 'ui' would be merged as is; currently it has two modes: only committed or all changes

- command for showing conflicts between current worktree and all other open worktrees

- command for showing all worktrees touching given file of interest

- agents getting real time notifications about potential conflicts

What is also important is that it works without an issue with all native git commands. Git sees those workspaces as normal worktrees. So you can e.g. normally rebase every such worktree separately (which is one of the main differences compared to overlayfs). I'm sure some people will think this project is very similar to GitFS, EdenFS, OverlayFS, ArtifactFS, etc... spoiler alert: it is not. Most of those projects are focusing on fetching objects from remote git server lazily. Which I can imagine is very useful if you need a fresh checkout on a new instance (eg. in a CI). But that is not my use case. I have a full local checkout, and need to be able to create and delete on demand a lot of worktrees. That is it :) But I also prepared a full comparison, just in case: https://github.com/pkukielka/gitfold/blob/main/docs/comparis...

I'm happy to answer any questions!

story_text.value:
In a rabbit hole learning about edible plants/fungi over the last few years I often would check inaturalist.org to see if certain species were nearby, and often wished I could just filter out edible species.

Over the past few months I've been working on creating a global database of edible (and to a lesser extent medicinal) species from many disparate sources, and edibilia.org cross references these with inaturalist (and a few other ocurrence data sources).

The map and taxa browser also include fairly powerful filters; ie filter by source (specific books, papers, websites), geographic filtering, morphological filtering, etc.

Lots to do still but I think its at a pretty useful point, happy for any feedback.
